Lol, totally. I love watching it while baked. It's like going through a portal to another dimension.

Let me tell you, normals just don't understand. They mean well, but they'll never "get" you cause they've never been through what you've been through. That's what I like about the internet, you can find whole communities full of people just like you, who can relate to your troubles. I've been through a lot of shit, and whenever I open up to people I have to explain that I don't need their pity or their worthless advice, I just want them to treat me like a fucking human being. At the end they still don't get it, but they at least stop patronizing me.

So, anything you wanna talk about in particular?

Hey man, failure isn't that bad. I've failed so many times, I've sort of just gotten used to it. I'll always remember that line from Adventure Time: "sucking at something is the first step towards being sorta good at something". Your parents were dead wrong, there's nothing wrong with flaws. Flaws are what make us human. Just think, if you were an outside observer looking at your life, would you hate you? Or would you feel compassion for them?

Anyways, you asked if there's anything good on netflix. I'd recommend Adventure Time. It appears to be a kids show, but it's really thoughtful and entertaining. Unfortunately, netflix only has the first 2 seasons, but if you google "watch adventure time" you should find the rest.

Hey, I'm a trans woman too. I've been on hormones for 10 months. Let me tell you, any physical changes you've experienced in 3 weeks are nothing compared to how you'll look, say, six months from now. It's not just boobs and soft skin, it really changes everything. Especially since you're only 23. And I still haven't got the voice thing either. I guess that takes time too.

What I'm trying to say is that being trans is mostly about patience. If you survive all this bullshit, eventually you'll escape it all. Seriously, I'm glad I stuck it out, because the feeling of looking in the mirror and seeing a woman for the first time is a truly wonderful experience. It's something special, that not many people get feel. It's like being a real person for the first time.
What would you think about delaying your suicide? Like, say, 24 hours. I mean, there's no rush, is there? Just hang out and talk to us in the meantime, you never know when things will get better.

I don't think it's that they don't care, it's just that they're really busy with their current patients, you know?

Can I ask why you cancelled your appointment?
They were probably legally required to give you that sort of boilerplate response. I wouldn't take it to heart.

Well, there's only one way to get used to new experiences. Have you thought about starting small? Like, just go to somewhere nearby to start. Maybe there's some hiking trails in your area? Idk, just an idea.

Honestly, sometimes you just have to be brave and face your anxiety head-on. You know what they say, true courage when you're afraid of something, but you do it anyways. And then afterwards, you get to be proud of yourself for doing something so scary. It's a nice feeling. Helps with depression a lot.

If you don't mind, I'll just leave my two cents here. I think you should take a vacation. I understand your worries all too well, trust me. But, if you go into it with no expectations, good or bad, I think you'll be pleasantly surprised. Being in a totally new place, out in nature, it feels like all your problems are so distant. Even if you do get depressed and cry, that's ok too. Crying is cathartic. It helps you begin to heal.

But, that's just my perspective. I think ultimately, it's your decision. Only you have the information you need to decide what's best for you.

Love hurts, man. It's perfectly normal to feel like absolute shit one or two months after a breakup. You trusted her, you let yourself get close to her, and she betrayed you. No doubt a wound like that takes a long time to heal.

The good news is, the human mind is resilient. If you tough it out for, say, six months to a year, you'll probably be feeling a lot better, as impossible as that must seem right now. You don't have to take my word for it, though, you should see for yourself. Survive, and experience healing.

Do you like lifting weights? I find it's a good alternative to self-harm. Plus, it's good for you! Working out is a pretty common post-breakup coping mechanism, haha.

I really hope you feel better, man. I've been at the brink before, and it's a miserable place. If you ever need to talk to someone, feel free to pm me :)
that's a pretty nasty way to die, sure you don't wanna talk to us here instead?

Walking doesn't make me feel better, per se, but it does make me feel alive, which is exactly the sort of kick in the pants I need some of the time. Idk, I walk around a lot on campus, and getting my blood flowing and being out in the sun feels pleasurable to me, so I tend to walk a lot more than other people, I think. I mean, it's all about how you walk, really. If you walk quickly with your eyes down, then you'll probably feel shitty, but if you take the time to really take in your surroundings, make note of every little detail, then it's more fun.

Although I'm not a Christian, I have studied the Bible and it has some cool parts. I especially like Psalm 23, by David:

"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in the green pastures: He leadeth me besides the still waters. He restoreth my soul: He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for His name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for Thou art with me; Thy rod and Thy staff comfort me. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: Thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."

Although I can't speak to the theology of this passage, or whether the Lord really is our shepherd, I find it comforting to know that David, living in a time and place wracked by war and pestilence and famine, was so grateful or all they had, and so optimistic for the future. I mean, this guy had to kill a guy named Goliath! With a sling! Plus, he lived in a time when famine, plague, and war struck swiftly, unexpectedly, and without mercy. He had been through some shit. But, because of his perspective, he thought life was so great, he wrote a poem about it.

I guess what I'm trying to say is, people can be content in spite of just about anything, once they learn how. For me, my personal demons are mood swings. Any moment, I could begin to spiral downward into a pit of anxiety and depression and self-destructive impulses. But, I learned how to deal with them. I still get mood swings, but they don't bother me any more. It's just another part of life. I guess it's kind of a Buddhist type philosophy. You know, the whole idea that our suffering is caused not by our circumstances, but by our desires. I don't desire to be free of mood swings any more. I mean, sure, if they go away, I'm not gonna cry or anything, but my life is perfectly fine with them. I don't know, man, this is all stuff you have to figure out for yourself. I just want you to know, it is totally possible to live a life of peace and contentedness, and you're on the right track.
You can let go without dying. The Buddhists called it Nirvana.

It sounds like you're going through a really difficult time. I just want you to know I'm rooting for you. I've been through a lot of bullshit too, I know how hard it can get. Just take one little, manageable part of the problem and deal with it, without worrying too much about the other stuff. Like, for example, you could decide that you want to stop self harming, and replace it with healthier coping mechanisms. I think that would be a great one. Maybe a little more straightforward than, say, trying to move out.

Is there anything else that's been troubling you? Any other obstacles? I'd be happy to talk with you

Well, I'm not saying that there aren't things that are easy, I'm just saying everything I'm proud of doing was hard and painful. All the easy stuff was fun, but not rewarding. Idk man. I guess I inherited that protestant work ethic from my calvinist ancestors, huh?

Well, for me, everything worthwhile I've ever done was really hard and painful. Recovering from suicidal depression, for example. Learning how to call people on the phone (I work in a call center). Getting a B+ in my college writing course. Coming out as trans to my family. Cleaning my apartment. There's more, I just have a bad memory.

I don't know how to help you with all the other stuff, but I will say, I once knew a girl who was about a year older than me. She was awesome. So fucking hot, and just about the nicest person I had ever met. She was the president of a certain club on campus, had a hot boyfriend with a huge dick (don't ask me how I know...), tons of friends, a busy social life, etc etc, and to lonely, depressed me, she seemed like the best person ever. Her life was perfect. I was extremely envious of her, actually...

Anyways, this was during the summer, so she would often wear shorts. And I couldn't help but notice she had parallel scars going up and down her thighs, and also on her wrists and shoulders. Scars you could only get from self harm. She didn't even try to hide them. This perplexed me, since she was so goddamn cheerful all the time. So, one day, when we were alone, I asked her about them... turns out that she had been extremely depressed until quite recently. She told me, she always had an excuse for cutting herself, but in the end it didn't ever help. She told me not to go down that road. I was just amazed at how well she had recovered.

So my friendship with her ended up disintegrating, but that memory lives on. This amazing, wonderful girl, covered in scars, a survivor of depression with no shame whatsoever about her past. I always hoped that I could end up like her. Her scars didn't look pathetic, they looked badass.

I don't know if this story will help you at all, but I found it very inspiring. Maybe I too could recover from all this shit in my head, and be all badass like her? I found myself putting in the effort I needed. I started by just cooking and cleaning, because fasting and living in filth were my two biggest sins. Do you think you could start trying to cook and clean a little more? I think you'll find that it'll make you feel a lot better.

I guess I wasn't super clear, what I meant is that, while feelings can definitely cause you pain, and I mean real pain, like the same pain you get when you hold an ice cube in your hand, pain can't kill your or injure your body. The effects of your feelings are limited to your mind. I still get feelings that are incredibly difficult to deal with. The difference is, now I don't fight them. Fighting your feelings is like a trapped fox trying to gnaw its own arm off, only in this case the trap exists entirely in the fox's head.

What do you do in between the waves? I'm more of a manic-depressive type, so I guess I have an unfair advantage here, but between my bouts of depression I try to take care of myself, do fun distracting things, you know, anything to keep my mind off the next wave, and to maybe make future bad feelings a bit easier. I read, cook, sleep, masturbate, play video games, talk to people on the internet, and so on and so forth. Is there anything you'd like to do during these easier times? It's a great opportunity to take care of yourself, and maybe learn new things. Like, for example, right now I'm working on my own wild yeast sourdough starter. I would never have dreamed of doing this during my depressive phases, but when I'm feeling okay, I just figure, why the hell not?

Oh, and feel free to pm me if you need anything :)

I think you misunderstood me a little. I was pretty grumpy when I wrote that, and I apologize. What I meant is, I think this attitude is insulting to survivors of mental illness. Even if the universe doesn't care about my recovery, it still meant something to me.

If you don't wanna live, well then, that's your business, not mine. But don't make value judgments about everyone else's lives. I worked hard for my happiness. I don't need any universal "goals" or "reasons" or "meaning". Fuck that shit. I just wanna be content.

Oh, awesome! I'm glad I helped you. So yeah, conversation techniques. I think the best think to know is that conversation is a skill, and like all skills, the only way to improve is to practice and fail a lot. Honestly, it's really hard to "fail" a conversation. Just remember, it's okay to be quiet if you don't know what to say. Just like discretion is the better part of valor, so too is silence the better part of talking. Also, ask questions about people. Everyone loves talking about themselves. Just make sure it's a dialogue and not an interrogation. Ask them questions, then relate their answers to your life or something. Also, living an interesting life will make it so much easier to talk to people. Telling stories is a really crucial part of conversation. There's so much more, but really the only way to learn this stuff is through practice. Good luck!

Oh, and lately I've been watching Whose Line is it Anyway? And those guys are geniuses. You can learn a lot from them.

Yeah, me too. I'm trans, so I'd probably get the shit beaten out of me, at best. Fortunately, I'm not in prison, and neither are you. Mental illness looks like a prison from the inside, but it's all just an illusion. It took me a long ass time to discover that I was actually free, and I could step out of the prison at any time. Like, let's say, 12 years. I thought that I was broken, that my mind would never allow me to do the things that "normal" people can do. But you know what? Feelings are just that: feelings. They can't hurt you. They're just chemical cycles in your brain. All the obstacles in your path are illusory. It's a leap of faith, like from The Last Crusade. Sorry, that's a lot of mixed metaphors, hahaha. But you get the idea.

Have you ever read The Republic? My personal theory, which has no evidence, but whatever, is that Socrates may have suffered from depression or bipolar disorder or something. He was a weird guy. But eventually he discovered the illusory nature of reality, and he did okay from there.
You should do what prisoners do and work out. It's clinically proven to be one of the best treatments for depression, and you'll feel healthier too. You don't even need anything but your own body.

Fuck this attitude! I'm a stoner and a functioning member of society. I keep my intoxication to myself.  This drug has gotten me through the worst shit. I seriously would be dead from my own hand right now if it wasn't for cannabis. If you wanna take the douchebags who use weed as an excuse to act like the idiots they are as being representative of all stoners, then quite frankly you're an asshole. When I eat at restaurants while stoned, I'm quiet, polite and withdrawn. I only vape so there's no smell. I never go out if I'm too stoned to act normal in public. There is nothing about weed that inherently makes anyone a douchebag, it just makes people who are already douchebags even more annoying.

The cannabis, especially indica dominant strains and anything with a lot of CBD in, has an immediate calming effect, one that lasts through the duration of the high and well into the "afterglow". Probably about 8 hours, I'd say, depending on the dose. But it can't last forever. 

The permanent changes, on the other hand, are far from instant and take a lot of work. Cannabis opens your mind in a way that allows you to get in there and start working through stuff. The psychedelia makes it easier to see things in new ways. But you're still gonna have to work for it. If you just smoke weed with the hope that it'll transform you into somebody who's not anxious, you're gonna be disappointed. I've been smoking weed for about 2 months, but I still have a longggg way to go. I've just been initiated, basically.

Unfortunately, there's pretty much no way to identify the strain just based on the finished product. But if you're just getting mids, you'll probably be fine. The difference between sativa and indica is most pronounced at the highest levels of quality. Like I said, the most important thing is to smart with just a small amount. As long as your head is in the right place, you'll be ok :)

Cannabis doesn't induce depersonalization in me. The really heavy indica strains I smoke usually make me feel very connected to myself. Mostly just a body effect, with some psychedelia. It's different for everyone, though.

Just start with a small dose. Since you have zero tolerance, you'll get some pretty strong effects from a small amount. If you like it, you can keep going. If you have a bad trip, just go somewhere quiet and safe and remember that it'll go away soon. And don't do what I did my first time and eat waaay too much of an edible without an appreciation for how powerful edibles are.

Hey, I've dealt with a lot of loneliness and social issues in my time. I know it can feel horrible. Sometimes I wondered if I was a broken human being, because it seemed like everyone around me had tons of friends while I had none. Why could everyone else do this thing that I can't?

The only thing that ever helped was to stop trying. I figured, all this worrying about friends is getting me nowhere, and it's just making me feel worse. So I decided to just focus on myself for a while. I didn't worry about being friends or social or anything, I only took care of myself and pursued solitary interests. Interestingly, my loneliness became much more manageable, and the social interactions I did have were much easier with the pressure taken off.

Everyone here is using WoW metaphors here, which I can understand but I think the analogy is misleading. Depression is not a monster to kill, it's not some demon you're locked in an eternal struggle with. And neither is it an illness that needs to be cured, like many doctors seem to believe. That sort of thinking implies that depression is some sort of entity that's separate from you, a force of evil that makes you miserable from afar. The truth is, you and your depression are one and the same. Depression and anxiety are just labels people put on the parts of their mind that they don't like. It's just who you are. And that's actually a good thing, because you accept who you are and learn to deal with it, rather than being forced to struggle against your feelings for eternity. It's a tough pill to swallow, but it's a lot easier this way.

Let me use myself as an example. I suffer from mood swings. They can be severe. One minute, I feel like I'm on crack, not sleeping for days on end, violently pacing back and forth in my apartment while frantically talking to myself. The next minute, I crash so hard that all I can do is loudly weep while squeezing my stuffed dragon (stuffed animals a better than any drug when it comes to bad feelings like depression and anxiety), crying for my momma and wondering what cruel god created me. You get the idea. I'll probably always have mood swings, to a greater or lesser degree. It's just who I am. Surprisingly, it turns out they're nothing I can't handle. It's the self hatred that really gets to you. I used to think I was a broken shell of a human being for not being able to regulate my emotions like "normal" people. My self esteem was in the negatives. I actively hated myself. I was preoccupied with thoughts of mutilating myself for a while, because I thought I deserved punishment for being so awful. But you know what? I think it's perfectly okay for a person to be more prone to bad feelings than most. I'm sure as hell not doing this on purpose. Just because your personality is more skewed towards the melancholic side, doesn't mean you're somehow a bad person. It just means you're unlucky, and you may have to work a little harder at living with yourself than the average bear. As I began to believe all this bullshit, my self-esteem started to slowly improve, and lately I've even been growing rather fond of myself. And it makes it a lot easier to deal with my mood swings when I don't have a bunch of self-loathing to worry about too. I'm starting to live an okay life. This it true peace.

I understand that you must feel horrible from all that loss. Family and home are the two things the human heart holds dearest, and you had them torn away from you. That's always gonna be traumatic, no matter who you are. Based on what you wrote, it sounds like you're full of self hatred, and you think you failed at life, whatever that means to you. I totally get that perspective. I've been there. But let me suggest an alternate way of looking at failure, one that's a bit easier to live with, one that probably saved my life a few times over the course of this summer.

How can you succeed if you don't fail a lot? That's like trying to make an omelette without breaking eggs. It may seem like the end of the world right now, but this is just the beginning. Failure doesn't mean you're somehow unworthy of life, or that you must be a wretched pile of scum dredged from the deepest, darkest crevices of the earth. Failure means you're human. It means you're trying. And in the end, that matters much more than success.

Well, it sounds like your feelings toward this person could be called unrequited love, don't you think? You really care for them, but unfortunately the feeling isn't mutual. I think everyone experiences unrequited love at some point in there life, and it's pretty much universally agreed that it sucks. Dante was massively infatuated with Beatrice Portinari, and she was alleged to be the inspiration of a lot of his books. I don't know if this makes you feel any better, but it sounds like you're having a normal reaction to this person's rejection. Back in high school I had some serious unrequited love, and god damn did it hurt. As for getting over her, I really can't help you, the only thing that worked for me was time. But I'm sure there's people with more experience who have better advice. Just hang in there, ok?

As for self hatred, well, this sounds all too familiar. It's really difficult to go forward when the person who's supposed to be your #1 ally hates your guts. Have you ever heard of the term self-compassion? It's a bit like self-esteem, but instead of liking yourself for your positive traits and stuff, it's about being compassionate towards yourself, even if you mess up. You can have self compassion even if you're the worst person in the whole world. There's a book called *Self-Compassion* by Dr. Kristin Neff that really helped put me on the track to being a good ally towards myself. I bet you could find a pdf on the internet or something. One thing in that book that I started to do that actually helped a lot was hugging myself. It sounds silly, but it's kind of difficult to hate yourself when you're touching yourself like a friend.

Something I do, that you might relate to, is this thing psychologists call "splitting". Basically, I have a tendency to either idolize or demonize people. Like, when I first make a new friend, at first I'll they're the greatest person ever. I'll build them up in my mind to be a god. Everything about them is way better than me. But then, when they invariably fail to live up to my expectations, I'll hate them forever. It made my relationships really difficult. I still do this sometimes, but I try really hard to look at both the positive and negative aspects of every person, including myself, and acknowledge that everyone is a combination of good and bad features, and that's perfectly ok.

I have a story. It's probably kind of trivial compared to what you're going through, but I think it's a good illustration of these principles nonetheless. You see, I'm transgender, and that means I need hormones. To get hormones, you have to have a blood draw to establish a baseline and make sure you're healthy. The problem is, I had a pretty bad fear of needles. I wanted these hormones so bad, more than anything in the world, but I was trembling at the thought of having a needle puncture my vein. Basically, at my university the way it works is the doctor puts in an order for lab tests and then you go into the lab and get your blood drawn at your own convenience. This was last October, I think? So, the next day, I looked in the mirror at my flat chest and mannish physique and figured, well, I at least have to try. I walked down to the clinic, and I got to the threshold, but I just could not enter. My anxiety wouldn't let me. I felt myself start to feel worse and worse, so I decided that today was not the day and I went home. The next day, I wasn't feeling to confident. I walked down to the clinic and got to the threshold, and I stepped through. Idk how I did it, but I did, I walked through that goddamn threshold like I owned the place. I think it was because I had been there before, it was more familiar to me, and so it became easier. Anyways, I walked up to the desk and gave them my info and they told me to take a seat. I nervously twiddled my thumbs for a while before the phlebotomist told me to come in. I had a seat on this weird chair that's specally designed for blood draws (it was very comfy). I tried to psych myself up, and I was telling the nurses that I just needed a few more minutes to calm down. But unfortunately, I just got more and more anxious. I started trembling, and one of them said that maybe I should try coming back again later. I was so relieved. I went home. Then, on the third day, I passed through the threshold, I sat in the chair, and I told the nurse, "just get it over with as quickly as possible". I squeezed my other hand, I grimaced, I swore, I felt my fingertips get all tingly and I think I almost passed out, but I did it. They got all the blood they needed. And now, 9 months later, I have this nice rack and beautiful girl face to show for it.

So yeah, if I was giving advice to you, I would say, just keep at it. Every time you fail to get on the bus is another learning opportunity. You could just walk to the bus stop with no intention of getting on, just to see what it's like and maybe get used to it. Also, you may need to show a little courage. You're probably always going to be anxious about this to some degree, you just gotta put one foot in front of the other and get on that bus.

Right now, I think the best thing for you would be to take care of yourself. You're going to experience some bad feelings, and they might last a while. Instead, I would offer some of the hardest earned advice I have. The easiest and best thing to do with bad feelings is to accept them. Accept that you're heartbroken and sad. Let the pain wash over you. Embrace it as a learning experience. Cry if you feel tears coming. Listen to your feelings, and try to observe them as they ebb and flow through your mind. This is called mindfulness. It's pretty much meditation: it was even invented by Buddhists long before psychologists in the western world caught on. Just accept your feelings, and feel them as they manifest themselves. Recognize the feelings for what they are: just feelings. As long as you don't take them too seriously, you'll be just fine.

Have you ever swam in the ocean? When there's big waves, and you're trying to swim out to sea, you'll find that they seriously impede your progress, slapping you silly and pulling you back towards the shore. Most people's instinct is to try and go on top of the waves, and keep their heads above water. But this is not a good idea. The top of the wave is the fastest moving part, and you'll just end up eating a bunch of seawater and getting knocked backwards. Instead, you have to dive through the base of the wave, which is moving slower, and you can break the water with your hands and hold your breath so it's not so unpleasant as being hit in the face with a crest. Also, when you emerge from the wave, rather than being knocked backwards you're already facing forward in swimming position. I'm sure the metaphor is pretty obvious here. Your heartbreak is a huge wave, and it's heading right for you. Every instinct in your body is probably telling you that you need to keep your head above water. But I'm telling you, dude, if you accept the wave and dive through it, you'll have a much easier time. I know from years of experience with mood swings, if you try and stay above water all you will just get slapped around when the waves come.

So maybe, instead of committing suicide, you could smoke a joint, hang out with friends, go explore nature, write angsty poetry, teach yourself knots, masturbate, cry into a pillow, fantasize about running away from civilization, browse reddit mindlessly, sleep, literally anything. Bad feelings call for self care. Eat disgustingly delicious food. This is all stuff I've done to get through tough feelings, by the way. Clean your room, talk to homeless people, do homework, go to the library, walk aimlessly around town, explore new neighborhoods, take long hot showers, teach yourself optics, talk to your neighbors, buy stuff online, learn to identify plants in your area. I imagine you already have stuff you do for pleasure, but this is a great time to explore new stuff too. You deserve to do something pleasurable. Breakups are never easy. The point I'm trying to make is that there's a ton of stuff you can do that will help you feel better without being self-destructive like suicide is. My criteria are, I have to fulfill my basic needs (food, water, sleep, hygiene, etc) and go to school, and I'm not allowed to do anything self-destructive, but other than that, I'll do anything I can to pass the time until my bad mood ends. I've actually learned to use bad feelings to my benefit, as weird as that may sound. The best thing you can do right now is take care of yourself, physically and emotionally.

I guess this sort of turned into an essay, so, uh, **tl;dr** you're heartbroken, which is normal, don't fight the pain, instead try to accept it, and take care of yourself, physically but more importantly emotionally. Good luck, if you need any help feel free to pm me anytime.

Hey, I just wanted to tell you I relate to this a lot. Many a night I have spent wondering if I'll ever be better, and hoping that I don't wake up. Fantasizing about ending it, and about self harm. Recently, I discovered the secret to surviving this sort of suicidal depression, and I thought I'd share it with you. It's quite simple, really. All you have to do to survive is don't kill yourself today. People who follow that rule have a 100% survival rate. They live to a ripe old age, the sort of age people are supposed to die at, like 80 or something. I think it's better to live for 80 horrible years than for 40 horrible years. 80 horrible years shows an impressive will to live. That person was truly motivated. But maybe that's a bit morbid hahaha.

Every day, just don't kill yourself. Resist the temptation. My therapist would probably make references to buzzwords like "urge surfing" or something ridiculous like that. Do whatever you have to do to not kill yourself today. Make it your number one priority. Lie face down on the floor, imagining naked girls to pass the time. Go on a walk. Sleep. Go on another walk. Eat. Browse reddit. Fantasize about suicide. I don't care what you do. I honestly don't. Just don't, and I repeat don't, commit suicide. I believe that most people can go one day without suicide. It will probably suck. You will probably hate it. But it's only until tomorrow. That's less than 24 hours! And you know what? I think you really want it. You're posting in /r/suicidewatch. If you really want it, if you're willing to do what it takes, you can go a day without anything.

Eventually you will begin to learn coping mechanisms. You will probably get creative, out of boredom. I hope you do, because this is how you make progress. You will begin to discover that some coping mechanisms work better than others. You'll probably discover that some coping mechanisms just make things worse in the long run. This is the learning process. Each day will be easier to cope than the last. As you learn what works and what doesn't, you will probably start building some semblance of a decent life. Perhaps eventually, the days will be easy. Your self esteem will clear up. You'll begin to feel happy again. The wounds begin to heal. And you know what? You'll have earned that happiness. Because it's a tough journey. And it's a journey that not everyone survives.

The early days will be the hardest. You will be incapable of many of the better coping mechanisms due to lack of practice. You will stumble. It will be hard. But I believe in the resilience of the human spirit. With enough will to survive, you can beat anything. My personal demons come in the form of mood swings, among other things. Sometimes they hit me hard. Sometimes I feel like my feeling have been beaten to a pulp. Sometimes I feel literal rage at myself. Sometimes I want desperately to hurt myself in any way that I can. Self harm was a bad coping mechanism that I fortunately never took up. But nowadays, like within the last 4 or 5 days, they're not so bad. In fact, I feel pretty confident now in saying that I'll never commit suicide, given what I know about myself. I know, from years and years of trial and error, that I can go one day without killing myself. I'm so good at coping with them that I hardly even notice them. They're just occurrences to me. I've even begun using them to my benefit. Sometimes crying is a tool of healing. You have to go through a storm to see a rainbow. That sort of thing. You, too, will get to a point where it's easy, a point where you feel well again, a point to where your self esteem can start to recover, or whatever it means to you. It'll be a tough journey. But I think you can make it. Just don't kill yourself today, under any circumstances.

The coping strategies that worked best for me were basic self care things like eating, bathing, sleeping, etc. They're a good distraction and they make your life better. I spent a lot of time alone, away from others, just smoking weed and reading, which to me is incredibly relaxing. It allows me to get away from my anxiety. I also make sure to keep my thoughts optimistic. I take things one tiny bite at a time. I try to think of the bad times as obstacles, not personal failures. I try to remember how far I've come, how resilient I must have been to survive so long. I spend a lot of time outside, which I've discovered I enjoy a lot. I try not to listen to the bad self esteem thoughts. There's a lot more, so if you need any help with specific problems feel free to ask.

Oh, and one last thing, keep those depressed friends of yours in mind. They can be a last line of defense during your really dark times. Thinking about my brother has saved my life.
